summary:
Space Vigil is an app that lets astronauts check their own health when no doctor can answer fast. On the way to Mars a message to Earth takes up to 24 minutes one way, so you need to know right away if something is off and what to do.

Every day the crew logs blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, SpO2, breathing, HRV, weight, exercise, stress and radiation dose, plus a reaction test and a camera pulse reading. The app compares each number to that person's own pre-flight baseline and to the official limits (NASA-STD-3001, ACC/AHA, CDC, ADA), then says in plain words: normal for you, keep an eye on it, or needs action, and why.

Every alert shows the rule, the numbers, the source, a checklist, and what the comm delay means for you right now. It works offline on a tablet and covers station, transit, rover and base. All crew data in the demo is simulated.
details:
What it does

Daily check-in (type the values or let the wearable prefill them), camera pulse, reaction test, trends with your personal baseline band and the official limits on the chart, alerts with checklists, a body map by 7 body systems and the 5 NASA hazards, a daily routine with reminders, a ground view showing what the flight surgeon receives after the light delay, CSV import, a Learn page explaining every number and source, and settings for 4 environments and 5 scenarios.

How it works

The 14 days before launch give a median and a median absolute deviation per indicator. In flight every value gets a robust z-score against that. More than about 3 typical deviations off, or 3 days drifting the same way, gets flagged even if the value would look fine for an average person. Published cut-offs sit on top. Each rule is a small TypeScript function tied to a source id, so anyone can read exactly what fires. Alerts also say what the delay means where you are: instant on a station, seconds at the Moon, up to 48 minutes round trip at Mars.

Why it matters

It catches slow drifts (sleep debt, slower reactions) before they become events, gets people measuring regularly, and packs the day into one message for the ground. If you rate yourself alert but your reaction test is slow, it tells you to trust the test: in ISS astronauts the two barely matched (Dev et al. 2024). Patches reward habits, never readings, so nobody gains by under-reporting.

Data source

Built around the Bio-Monitor (Hexoskin Astroskin) shirt flown on the ISS since 2019: ECG, HR, HRV, breathing, SpO2, skin temperature, activity, sleep. Cuff, glucose meter and dosimeter are typed or imported. The prototype uses simulated values in that shape.

Method and tools

Design thinking with 3 users (astronaut, crew medical officer, flight surgeon) and one goal: understand an alert and the next step in under 30 seconds. React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Recharts, vitest. No backend. GitHub Pages.

Checks and limits

All 37 alert rules are tested at their boundary and every cited source is checked to exist (docs/VALIDATION.md). It's decision support, not a medical device: no diagnosis, no drug advice. The reaction test isn't lab-validated and the camera pulse is experimental. Next step: a version a flight surgeon configures per crew member, with a real wearable feeding it.
